hints: Break the formula $\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6\text{Cl}_3$ into atoms: 1 Cr plus 6 waters plus 3 Cl, then recall $A_r$ values for Cr, H, O and Cl.
walkthrough:
Add up the building blocks**
Think of $\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6\text{Cl}_3$ as one Cr, plus six whole water molecules, plus three chlorines. Water has $M_r = 2(1.0) + 16.0 = 18.0$. So you have $$M_r = A_r(\text{Cr}) + 6 \times M_r(\text{H}_2\text{O}) + 3 \times A_r(\text{Cl})$$ $$= 52.0 + 6 \times 18.0 + 3 \times 35.5 = 266.5$$

hints: Only chloride ions outside the complex, the $(3-n)$ $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, can precipitate as $\text{AgCl}$. Coordinated Cl bound to Cr does not react.
First find moles of complex in 1.00 g using your $M_r$, then compare with moles of $\text{AgCl}$ formed to find how many free $\text{Cl}^-$ per formula unit, which equals $3-n$.
walkthrough:
Separate bound chloride from free chloride**
Picture the general formula $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_{6-n}\text{Cl}_n]\text{Cl}_{3-n}.n\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The $n$ chlorides inside the square brackets are directly bonded to $\text{Cr(III)}$ and are inert to $\text{Ag}^+$. Only the $(3-n)$ chlorides outside as counter ions dissolve as $\text{Cl}^-(\text{aq})$ and give $$\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Cl}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(\text{s})$$ So moles of $\text{AgCl}$ tells you $(3-n)$ directly.

Find moles of complex in the sample**
You weighed 1.00 g of every isomer: $$n(\text{complex}) = \frac{1.00}{266.5} = 3.75 \times 10^{-3} \text{ mol}$$ This is your baseline. Every 1.00 g contains the same number of formula units because all isomers share the same $M_r$.

Use the ratio to get n**
Take isomer A: $3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $\text{AgCl}$ is formed from $3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol complex, a 1:1 ratio. So $3-n = 1$ and $n = 2$. That gives $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Cl}.2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. For B, $7.50 \times 10^{-3} / 3.75 \times 10^{-3} = 2$ free chlorides, so $3-n = 2$, $n = 1$. For C, $1.13 \times 10^{-2} / 3.75 \times 10^{-3} = 3$ free chlorides, so $3-n = 3$, $n = 0$.

Final answer: Moles of complex in 1.00 g $= 1.00/266.5 = 3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol.
A: $3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol $\text{AgCl}$ per $3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ mol complex = 1 free $\text{Cl}^-$, so $3-n = 1$, $n = 2$, $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_4\text{Cl}_2]\text{Cl}.2\text{H}_2\text{O}$
B: $n = 1$, $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2.\text{H}_2\text{O}$
C: $n = 0$, $[\text{Cr}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]\text{Cl}_3$

hints: Focus on the fact that the same four ligands around Ni can be arranged with identical ligands next to each other or opposite each other, giving different polarity.
walkthrough:
Recognise the spatial swap**
You have $\text{Ni}(\text{R}_3\text{P})_2(\text{CN})_2$ with two pairs of identical ligands. When the same ligands can be adjacent or opposite without breaking bonds, with one form polar and one non-polar, that is the classic signature of geometric, also called cis-trans, isomerism.

hints: Ni(II) with 4 ligands here is square planar, so draw Ni at the centre of a square with the four ligands at the corners, placing the two $\text{CN}$ groups opposite in one isomer and adjacent in the other.
walkthrough:
Draw the square planar framework**
Place $\text{Ni}$ in the centre with four positions: top, bottom, left, right. This complex is square planar, not tetrahedral, so flat 90 degree angles matter.
Isomer 1, trans: put $\text{CN}$ top and $\text{CN}$ bottom, and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ left and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ right. Identical ligands are opposite.
Isomer 2, cis: put $\text{CN}$ top and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ bottom, and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ left and $\text{CN}$ right. Identical ligands are at 90 degrees, on the same side.

Final answer: Isomer 1 (trans): $\text{CN}$ opposite $\text{CN}$ and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ opposite $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ around square planar Ni.
Isomer 2 (cis): $\text{CN}$ adjacent to $\text{CN}$ and $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ adjacent to $\text{R}_3\text{P}$ around square planar Ni.

hints: Think about symmetry: if identical polar $\text{Ni-CN}$ bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions they cancel, but if they point at 90 degrees they reinforce.
walkthrough:
Link symmetry to polarity**
The $\text{Ni-CN}$ bonds are polar. In the trans isomer the two $\text{CN}$ dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel exactly, and the two $\text{Ni-PR}_3$ dipoles also cancel, so the molecule is non-polar overall. In the cis isomer both $\text{CN}$ groups lie on the same side, their dipoles add to give a net dipole moment. So isomer 2 is the polar one.
Final answer: Isomer 2 (cis isomer) has a dipole moment because the $\text{CN}^-$ groups are on the same side so bond dipoles do not cancel.
